title: Scripts: running, parameters & exit codes
about: Writing and running shell scripts: the shebang, execute permission, the ways to launch a script and what each one does to your shell, positional parameters, exit statuses, reading input, messages and scheduling with cron.

questions.title: From idea to running script
questions.text: Put the steps of creating and running your first script in order.

items.t: Write the commands into a file, starting with `#!/bin/bash`
items.why: The file must exist first, and the first line selects the interpreter.

items.t: Give it execute permission with `chmod u+x script.sh`
items.why: Without `x` the kernel refuses to run it directly.
The `./` is needed when the current directory is not in `PATH`.

items.t: Check `echo $?` to see whether it succeeded
items.why: The exit status of the script is available right afterwards.

questions.title: The shebang line
questions.text: What does the first line `#!/bin/bash` of a script do?

options.t: It tells the kernel which interpreter to start to run the file when the script is executed directly.
options.why: The kernel reads the two characters `#!` and runs the named program with the script as its argument.

options.t: It is a comment with no effect at all, because it begins with `#`.
options.why: Only when the script is run as `bash script` does the line act as a comment.

options.t: It imports the `bash` library into the script.

questions.title: Missing shebang
questions.text: A script has no shebang line and execute permission. You run `./script.sh` from bash. What usually happens?

options.t: Bash runs it with itself (a new shell), treating the file as a shell script.
options.why: The kernel cannot identify an interpreter, so the calling shell falls back to running it as a script.
The file was found; the failure would be about permissions.
Nothing is printed unless the script does it.

questions.title: Comments
questions.text: Which line of a script is a comment?

options.why: From a `#` at the start of a word to the end of the line.

questions.title: Making it executable
questions.text: Allow the owner to run `run.sh` directly: `chmod {{0}} run.sh`
questions.note: Without an `x` bit, `./run.sh` fails with "Permission denied".

wrong.why: That gives read and write but no execute permission.
Read is not what is missing.

questions.title: Permission denied
questions.text: `./run.sh` prints "Permission denied" although the file exists and you own it. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.t: The file has no execute permission; run `chmod u+x run.sh`.
options.why: Or start it with `bash run.sh`, which needs only read permission.
Unix does not use extensions for that.

options.t: The script must be copied to `/bin` first.

options.why: Owners can run their own scripts.

questions.title: Name lookup
questions.text: A script `tool.sh` is in your current directory (not in `PATH`). Typing `tool.sh` gives "command not found". Why does `./tool.sh` work?

options.t: A name with a slash is a path, so no `PATH` search is made; a bare name is searched only in the `PATH` directories.
options.why: The current directory is deliberately not in `PATH` by default.

options.t: `./tool.sh` works only for files owned by root.

questions.title: How a script is launched
questions.text: Classify each way of starting `script.sh`.

items.bucket: Runs in a new child shell
items.why: The kernel starts the interpreter as a new process.

items.bucket: Runs in a new child shell
Runs in a new child shell

items.why: The commands run as if typed at the prompt.
The dot is a synonym for `source`.
A typical use: reload the configuration.

buckets: Runs in a new child shell

questions.title: cd inside a script
questions.text: A script contains `cd /tmp`. You run `./script.sh` and afterwards type `pwd`. Where are you?

options.t: Still in the directory you started from, because the script's `cd` changed the directory of its own child process.
options.why: Use `source script.sh` to change the directory of your shell.

questions.title: source and cd
questions.text: The same script run with `source script.sh` (containing `cd /tmp`). Where are you afterwards?

options.why: The commands ran in your own shell, so its working directory changed.

questions.title: PIDs tell the story
questions.text: A script prints `$$`. Run with `bash script.sh` several times, the number changes each time; run with `source script.sh`, it equals the PID of your shell. What does this show?

options.t: `bash script.sh` creates a new process each time, while `source` runs the commands inside the existing shell process.
options.why: `$$` is the PID of the shell executing the commands.

options.t: `source` creates a new process that happens to reuse the PID.

options.why: It is the real process ID.

questions.title: Things that only `source` can do
questions.text: Select what works only if the script is sourced (run with `source` or `.`).

options.t: Changing the current directory of your interactive shell.
options.why: The child of `./script` cannot do that.

options.t: Setting a variable that stays available afterwards in your shell.
options.why: Variables of a child die with it.

options.t: Defining a function or alias that you can use from the prompt afterwards.
options.why: Definitions live in the shell that ran them.

options.t: Reading arguments given on the command line.
options.why: Both ways can use arguments (with `source`, they become the script's parameters).

questions.title: Running without exec bit
questions.text: Which command runs `script.sh` even though it has no execute permission (only read)?

options.why: Bash opens the file as data and interprets it.
The kernel insists on an `x` bit.

questions.title: Exit from source
questions.text: A script contains `exit 1` on its first line. What happens when you run it with `source script.sh` in your terminal?

options.t: Your interactive shell exits (the terminal may close), because `exit` ended the shell that ran the commands.
options.why: Use `return` in sourced scripts, or run them normally.

options.t: Only the script stops and you get the prompt back.
An error message about the exit code.
options.why: No error; the shell simply exits.

questions.title: Special parameters
questions.text: Match each special parameter with its content.

pairs.r: The name the script was invoked with

pairs.why: `$2` is the second, and so on.

pairs.r: All the arguments, as separate words (when quoted)
The exit status of the last command
The PID of the shell running the script

extras.r: The user who runs the script

questions.title: Count of arguments
questions.text: For `./s.sh "one two" three`, what is `$#`?

options.why: The quoted string is one argument and `three` is the other.

questions.title: Star versus at
questions.text: For `./s.sh "a b" c`, what is the difference between `for x in "$@"` and `for x in $*`?

options.t: `"$@"` iterates twice (`a b` and `c`), while unquoted `$*` splits on blanks and iterates three times (`a`, `b`, `c`).

options.why: It produces one word per argument.

questions.title: The four forms
questions.text: For `./s.sh "a b" c`, match each expression with the words it produces.

pairs.why: Joined with the first character of `IFS`.
Both are subject to word splitting, so the quotes of the original arguments are lost.

extras.why: Not produced by any of them.

questions.title: The loop without in
questions.text: What does `for i; do echo "$i"; done` iterate over inside a script?

options.t: The positional parameters, like `for i in "$@"`.
options.why: When `in` is omitted, the list is the arguments.

options.t: The files of the current directory.
The lines typed at the keyboard.
Nothing, it is a syntax error.

questions.title: shift
questions.text: What does `shift` do to the positional parameters?

options.t: It discards `$1` and renumbers: `$2` becomes `$1`, `$3` becomes `$2`, and `$#` decreases by one.
It rotates them, moving `$1` to the end.
It shifts the digits of the numbers.

questions.title: Processing every argument
questions.text: Which loop processes all the arguments of a script one by one, even if there are more than nine?

options.why: Uses `$1` each time and then moves on.
Runs only when there are no arguments.

questions.title: Tenth argument
questions.text: Why is the tenth argument written `${10}` and not `$10`?

options.t: `$10` is read as `$1` followed by the character `0`; braces mark where the parameter number ends.
Because bash supports at most nine arguments.
`$10` is the exit status of the last command.

questions.title: Count and name
questions.text: Inside a script, the number of arguments it received is in `{{0}}`, and the name it was called with is in `{{1}}`.
questions.note: `$#` never includes the script name, which is `$0`.

wrong.why: That is the list of all the arguments, not their number.
That is the exit status of the last command.

questions.title: Missing argument
questions.text: The script uses `$1`, but the user runs it with no arguments. What is `$1`?

options.t: Empty, unless `set -u` is active; bash does not complain about missing positional parameters.
options.why: That is why scripts should check `$#` before using them.
An unset parameter is just empty.

options.t: The bash aborts with an error at once.

questions.title: Default values
questions.text: Which expression gives `$1` when it was provided and the text `default` otherwise?

options.why: The `:-` form substitutes a default for unset or empty values.
The opposite: use `default` only if `$1` is set.
Assignment to a positional parameter is not allowed.

questions.title: Usage check at the top
questions.text: Put the steps of a well-behaved script start in order.

items.t: Check the number of arguments with `[ $# -ne 1 ]`
items.why: Nothing else makes sense without the right input.

items.t: Print a usage message to standard error
items.why: Tell the user what is expected.

items.t: Only then continue with the real work
items.why: The main part runs after validation has passed.

questions.title: Exit values
questions.text: What is the exit status of a script that ends without an explicit `exit`?

options.t: The status of the last command it executed.
options.why: So a trailing `echo` makes a failing script look successful.
Only if the last command succeeded.

options.t: Undefined, the shell refuses to finish.

questions.title: Choose the code
questions.text: Which use of exit codes is conventional?

options.t: 0 for success and small non-zero numbers (1, 2, 3...) for different kinds of failure.
options.why: Callers can branch on the number.

questions.title: Range of exit codes
questions.text: What does `exit 256` produce as the script's exit status?

options.t: 0, because exit statuses are taken modulo 256 (the low 8 bits).

questions.title: exit versus return
questions.text: What is the difference between `exit` and `return` inside a function of a script?

options.t: `return` leaves only the function (giving a status to the caller), while `exit` ends the whole script.
options.why: `return` outside a function or sourced script is an error.

options.t: `return` ends the script and `exit` ends the function.

questions.title: Status of the last command
questions.text: After `grep -q root /etc/passwd`, what does `echo $?` print if `root` is present?

options.why: Grep succeeds when it finds a match.

questions.title: Saving the status
questions.text: Why save the status with `rc=$?` before running other commands?

options.t: `$?` is overwritten by every command, including `echo`, so it must be copied if you need it later.
options.why: Otherwise you would test the status of the `echo`.

options.t: Because `$?` is read-only after the first use.
Because bash deletes it at the end of the line.
options.why: It stays until the next command.

questions.title: The if and the status
questions.text: What does `if cp a b; then echo copied; fi` test?

options.t: The exit status of `cp`: the `echo` runs when it is 0.
options.why: Any command can be the condition of an `if`.

options.t: Whether the text `cp a b` is non-empty.

questions.title: Error messages
questions.text: Why should error messages be written to standard error (`>&2`)?

options.t: So that they are not mixed with the normal output when a caller redirects or pipes stdout.
options.why: A caller can capture results separately from diagnostics.

options.t: Because `echo` refuses to write to stdout after a failure.

questions.title: After an error, stop
questions.text: Why does a script normally exit right after printing an error such as "file not found"?

options.t: Continuing would run later commands on missing or invalid input, possibly causing damage or hiding the problem.
options.why: Fail early, with a non-zero status.

options.t: Because bash forbids any command after `echo`.

options.why: Writing to stderr does not stop anything.

options.t: Because the exit status must be reset.

questions.title: Good exit handling
questions.text: Select the statements that describe good practice in a script.

options.t: Validate the arguments first and exit with a non-zero status on bad input.
options.why: So callers can detect the problem.

options.t: Use different exit codes for different kinds of errors when a caller may care.
options.why: For example 1 for usage, 2 for a missing directory.

options.t: Check the status of commands whose failure would make later steps meaningless.
Ignore the status of `rm -rf "$DIR"/*` because it is obviously fine.
options.why: Dangerous when `DIR` is empty or wrong.

questions.title: Stop if cd fails
questions.text: Do not continue when the directory cannot be entered: `cd "$DIR" {{0}} exit 1`
questions.note: `cd "$DIR" || { echo "no such dir" >&2; exit 1; }` adds a message.

questions.title: Exit on any error
questions.text: What does `set -e` do in a script?

options.t: The script exits as soon as a simple command fails (with some exceptions such as commands in conditions).
options.why: A crude safety net; explicit checks remain clearer.

options.t: It enables the shell's error messages.
It prints every command before running it.

questions.title: Reading input
questions.text: Which command asks the user for a line and stores it in `ANS`?

options.why: Reads one line from standard input into the variable.

questions.title: Prompt in read
questions.text: Ask the question and read the answer on one line: `read {{0}} "Overwrite? (s/n) " ANSWER`
questions.note: `-r` is also advisable: it prevents backslashes from being interpreted.

wrong.why: That hides the typing (for passwords) but shows no prompt.
That limits the number of characters to read.

questions.title: read splitting
questions.text: After `read a b c <<< "one two three four"`, what is in `c`?

options.why: Extra words go to the last variable.
The last variable takes the remainder.
The last variable receives everything left.

questions.title: Reading a file line by line
questions.text: Which loop reads a file line by line and keeps the variables set inside it after the loop?

options.why: The redirection feeds the loop without a subshell.

options.t: `cat file | while read line; do ...; done`
options.why: The pipe makes the loop a subshell whose changes are lost.
That iterates over the single word `file`.

questions.title: for over lines
questions.text: Why is `for line in $(cat file)` a poor way to read lines?

options.t: It splits the content on any blank, not only newlines, so lines with spaces are broken into several words.
It cannot read more than ten lines.
It is faster than `while read`, which is why it is discouraged.

questions.title: Quote variables
questions.text: Why should you write `rm "$file"` instead of `rm $file`?

options.t: Without quotes, a value with spaces or wildcards is split into several arguments and expanded, possibly deleting the wrong files.
options.why: Quote every expansion unless you want splitting.

options.t: Quotes are required in every command.

questions.title: Arithmetic on variables
questions.text: Which line stores `DATOA*DATOB+5` in `R` using shell arithmetic?

options.why: Command substitution would try to run a command.
Assigns text; the pipe does nothing for `R`.

questions.title: Numbers are strings
questions.text: What is the value of `X` after `X=5; X=$X+1`?

options.why: Without arithmetic expansion the shell just concatenates.

questions.title: Information commands
questions.text: Match each command with the information it gives, as a script might show at start.

pairs.r: The name of the user running the script
The version of the running bash

questions.title: Relative paths
questions.text: A script uses the relative path `data/in.txt`. From which directory is it resolved?

options.t: The current working directory of the process running the script, which is where the user was when launching it.
options.why: Not the directory where the script is stored.

options.t: The directory that contains the script file.

options.why: Only if the user was there.

questions.title: Script directory
questions.text: Which expression gives the directory that contains the running script (for a script called by path)?

options.why: That gives the file name only.
The current directory of the caller.

questions.title: Path helpers
questions.text: Match each command with its result for `/home/alumno/docs/a.txt`.

pairs.r: The absolute form of the path

extras.why: None of the commands above returns only the parent's name.

questions.title: The cron fields
questions.text: Match each field of a `crontab` line (`m h dom mon dow command`) with its position and meaning.

pairs.r: Day of the week (0-7, where 0 and 7 are Sunday)

questions.title: Every four hours
questions.text: Which crontab schedule runs a command every four hours, on the hour?

options.why: Minute 0, every fourth hour, every day.

questions.title: Edit your crontab
questions.text: Which command opens your personal crontab for editing?

options.why: The entries run with your user's privileges.
`cron` is the daemon, not the editor.

questions.title: Log the result
questions.text: A line in a crontab should append both normal output and errors of `/home/alumno/ipLog.sh` to a log. Which command field is correct?

options.why: Use absolute paths; cron runs with a minimal environment.
Relative names and overwriting; the errors are lost.
The redirections cannot precede the command this way.
A pipe needs a command on the right.

questions.title: Cron environment
questions.text: Why does a script that works in your terminal sometimes fail when run by cron?

options.t: Cron runs it with a minimal environment (short `PATH`, no interactive startup files), so commands or relative paths may not be found.
options.why: Use absolute paths and set variables inside the script.

options.t: Cron uses a different file system.
Cron refuses scripts longer than ten lines.

questions.title: Who sees the output
questions.text: Where does the normal output of a cron job go if you do not redirect it?

options.t: It is typically sent by mail to the job's owner, if a mail system is configured.
options.why: That is why most cron lines redirect output to a file.

options.t: To the terminal of the user.
To the syslog automatically, with nothing mailed.

questions.title: Logs
questions.text: Which file usually records authentication events (logins, `sudo`, failed SSH attempts) on a Debian-based system?

options.why: Text lines with date, host, service and message.
